scenes.visual: Title card: Which Neurons Get the Message. Show a cochlear implant stimulating surviving auditory neurons, then small retinal and touch interface schematics.

scenes.tts: A cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells and stimulates surviving auditory neurons. It gives many adults with severe hearing loss useful hearing. That is the clinical payoff: electrical stimulation can support speech understanding. The implant borrows the cochlea's frequency map. Higher frequencies go to basal contacts, lower ones to apical contacts. Which neurons get which information? That question runs through sensory prostheses.

scenes.visual: Begin with damaged hair cells and surviving auditory neurons. Animate an implant bypassing the hair cells and exciting the neurons; show speech understanding as the functional benefit. Reveal the cochlear place map, labelling basal contacts as higher frequency and apical contacts as lower frequency. End on the question: Which neurons get which information?

scenes.tts: A contact is hardware. A channel is a band of frequency information. Neighbouring contacts produce overlapping electric fields, called channel interaction. So more contacts do not mean as many independent channels. Useful sensation depends on which surviving neurons receive the signal and the pattern it carries. Electrode count alone cannot tell us that.

scenes.visual: Enlarge neighbouring contacts on the cochlear array. Label a contact as hardware and a channel as a frequency band. Draw overlapping electric fields reaching overlapping neural populations. Distinguish the hardware, information and recruited neurons without displaying a numerical channel ceiling.

scenes.tts: In the retina, targeting shapes what people see. An electrode on the inner surface sits beside ganglion-cell axons passing toward the optic disk. Implant users often drew elongated or distorted shapes from single electrodes. An axon-pathway model accounted for those shapes. This is a model-supported explanation, not a direct recording. One electrode does not make one pixel.

scenes.visual: Show an epiretinal electrode over ganglion-cell axons running toward the optic disk. Contrast a tempting single-dot expectation with elongated or distorted percept drawings. Animate axons of passage only as a schematic model, labelled model-supported explanation, not recorded activity. Keep percepts distinct from the anatomical sketch.

scenes.tts: Retinal implants can provide limited vision after photoreceptor loss. In the PRIMA design, pixels beneath the retina turn projected near-infrared light into current that stimulates bipolar cells. The signal then passes through the remaining retinal network. Early participants with optimal chip placement achieved prosthetic acuity. Later trial benefits came with serious device- or procedure-related events.

scenes.visual: Introduce PRIMA as a different, subretinal route. Show a camera image projected as near-infrared light onto photovoltaic pixels beneath the retina, then current to bipolar cells and signals through the remaining inner retinal network. Pair a limited prosthetic-acuity benefit in participants with optimal placement with a later-trial serious-event notice. Do not show normal sight, responder fractions, acuity calculations or a claimed advantage over epiretinal implants.

scenes.tts: Optogenetics changes the surviving cells. A viral vector makes them express a light-sensitive protein. In one adult with retinitis pigmentosa, treated ganglion cells responded to light from engineered goggles. With the treated eye and goggles, the patient located, counted and touched objects. Without the goggles, the patient did not detect objects. This was partial, goggle-dependent function in one person, not normal vision.

scenes.visual: Show surviving retinal ganglion cells acquiring a light-sensitive protein, then engineered goggles converting the scene into bright amber light patterns. Compare the reported object tasks with the treated eye and goggles against failure to detect objects without goggles after treatment. Label the evidence as one participant and partial, goggle-dependent function; do not depict normal vision.

scenes.tts: Touch can be written into a peripheral nerve or into sensory cortex. Nerve stimulation produced phantom-hand touch in people with amputations and helped them handle delicate objects. In one man with a spinal cord injury, motor-cortex signals controlled a robotic arm. Stimulation of sensory cortex supplied touch feedback and shortened his task time. That supports feedback for this person, not a population effect.

scenes.visual: First show a residual peripheral nerve receiving stimulation, a phantom-hand touch percept and delicate-object handling with a prosthesis. Then show a separate spinal-cord-injury example: motor-cortex signals drive a robotic arm and somatosensory stimulation returns touch feedback. Highlight less time spent trying to grasp, with the one-participant scope beside the benefit. Keep the peripheral and cortical populations distinct.

scenes.tts: The design rule is to reproduce task-relevant features of the natural neural code, then test perception and behaviour. Biomimicry is an evidence-backed strategy. It is not a proven law that more exact copying always improves performance.

scenes.visual: Bring back the cochlear place map, retinal targets, optogenetic goggles and bidirectional arm interface. Connect them to task-relevant neural coding, then to tests of perception and behaviour. Label biomimicry as an evidence-backed design strategy, without claiming universal superiority or ranking the devices across disorders.
End card: Which neurons get which information? Test the percept. Test the behaviour.
